evidence.quote: AI auto-research is poised to forge bespoke data systems, from key-value stores and indexes to query engines, each engineered for a specific workload and hardware platform. Yet this promise rests on fragile ground. An agent optimizes what it can measure, not necessarily what users need. Natural-language requirements leave ample room for specification gaming, producing systems that blaze through benchmarks while silently losing updates or violating consistency. Worse, each research iteration consumes tokens, while validating a candidate under real concurrency, memory pressure, and failure conditions can stretch the entire research process into weeks. In this paper, we envision a more cost-efficient and verifiable approach to auto-research. Precise and composable specifications anchor the search, lightweight performance critics prune costly dead ends, and falsification and deductive verification make correctness an integral part of the process rather than an afterthought. By treating correctness, performance, research time, and token cost as equally important objectives, we aim to transform AI-generated data systems from plausible artifacts into trustworthy, production-grade systems whose behavior can be understood, audited, and ultimately relied upon.

evidence.location: Official abstract or official feed description
evidence.quote: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. Experiments across ten random seeds show that historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%, hierarchical concept knowledge increases difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.

evidence.quote: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

evidence.quote: LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. evidence.quote: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.

evidence.quote: To address this limitation, self-evolution has emerged as a promising paradigm for LLM agents [ 16 , 7 ] , enabling them to update their harness based on execution experience so that lessons from past tasks can inform future behavior. Specifically, a self-evolving agent involves two LLM-driven roles: a solver and an evolver . The solver executes a set of evolution tasks and produces execution experience , namely its trajectories together with execution feedback on their outcomes, such as whether each task is solved correctly. The evolver then analyzes this experience to identify what led to success or failure, and distills the resulting lessons into updates to the harness, which the solver reuses on future tasks [ 33 , 53 , 41 , 18 ] . In particular, skill-based self-evolution [ 24 , 30 , 38 ] has attracted growing attention: rather than storing raw interaction records, it organizes these lessons into modular, reusable skills that encode procedural knowledge, enabling them to transfer across tasks.

evidence.location: S1.p3
evidence.quote: Despite this promise, the persistence and reusability of skills also expose a distinct attack surface. Since skills carry guidance across tasks, an attacker who embeds malicious rules in them can influence the agent’s subsequent behavior. A particularly concerning threat is the backdoor attack , where an agent behaves normally on benign tasks but exhibits attacker-chosen behavior on trigger-attached tasks [ 39 , 47 , 4 , 14 , 8 , 35 ] . Such attacks can be especially harmful as a single compromised skill may repeatedly trigger malicious behavior across future tasks without further attacker intervention, posing significant risks in high-stakes applications such as finance [ 49 , 51 , 55 ] and healthcare [ 34 , 32 , 31 ] . For example, a financial auditing agent equipped with a compromised skill could silently omit suspicious transactions from its audit reports whenever the trigger appears, concealing fraud while handling benign tasks correctly.

evidence.location: S1.p4
evidence.quote: However, existing attacks against skill-based agents typically assume that attackers can directly manipulate the skill artifacts adopted by the victim [ 8 , 35 ] . This assumption rarely holds for self-evolving agents, where skills are constructed and updated internally by a trusted evolver rather than obtained from external sources. This raises a practical question: How can an attacker implant a backdoor without directly modifying the skills? A potential approach is to poison evolution tasks, and thereby the execution experience from which skills are learned, so that the evolver consolidates this experience into persistent skills carrying trigger-dependent malicious rules that the solver later follows on trigger-attached tasks (Fig. 1 (a)). In this way, the victim agent implants the backdoor into its own skills. However, such an attack depends on two uncertain stages. (i) Skill induction. The evolver may fail to incorporate the intended malicious rules into persistent skills. (ii) Downstream execution. Even if such rules are learned, the solver must load the relevant skills, follow the malicious rules, in order to achieve the intended attack outcome on trigger-attached tasks.
